reason: The text depicts Yahweh as a covenant God who responds conditionally to the Hebrew people's faithfulness or breach of covenant, rather than as inherently antagonistic. While the text contains divine judgment against Judah for covenant violation (Hulda's prophecy of coming destruction), this is presented as just punishment for specific breaches, not arbitrary hostility. Significantly, King Josiah—a Hebrew ruler—is shown receiving divine favor and protection: because 'your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before Yahweh' (יַ֠עַן רַךְ־ לְבָ֨בְךָ֜), Yahweh grants him peace in death and removes him from witnessing the coming judgment. The text further praises Josiah as unmatched among kings for turning to Yahweh 'with all his heart and all his soul and all his might' (וְכָמֹהוּ֩ לֹֽא־ הָיָ֨ה). This demonstrates that Yahweh's posture toward the Hebrew people is relational and responsive to repentance, not antagonistic. The judgment on Judah is presented as a consequence of their idolatry and covenant-breaking, not evidence of antipathy.
